title: Joining the Musicians Union and Local 767
summary: He joined in late 1927 when the Black local 767 met in a garage, with few benefits and little enforcement compared with white Local 47.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: I think you mentioned that it was somewhere around then that you joined the Musician's Union, wasn't it?

'27, yes, I joined the Musician's Union in the latter part of 1927, and it was very new at that time. In fact, our union office was in the garage of one of the fellows, back in the alley there off of Central Avenue.
And was the -- in those days there were
(the black local and the white local --(inaudible) the 767 and 47.
The 47, yes, I'm pretty sure it was.
And was the one that was in the (47) garage.
Right. Right, uh-huh. And later they moved to a house on Central Avenue.
Do you know what year that 767 was formed (inaudible)?
No, I don't. It was before me, because they didn't have a house, or they didn't have an office. We all went in this fellow's garage and paid our dues and things like that.
I don't even remember that. It was very little. I know that.
Was the union really active then? Did it go around and check and see whether places were hiring union members?

No. No. It didn't do much work such as union work then. It was just getting started, and they were just trying to cultivate a membership more than enforce the laws and bylaws. I think 47 was fairly well situated, but they just looked on 767 as, oh, well, they're over there, and
they get what they can or what's left over and -- So at that point in those days there weren't many benefits from being --
